articles.headline: The Rays are making too many mistakes to stand a chance against the relentless Brewers
keyFacts: The Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays 5-4 in Game 2 of the World Series after overcoming an early four-run deficit.
Rays manager Kevin Cash stated that his team did not play their cleanest baseball game and made multiple costly mistakes.
The Brewers currently hold a 2-0 lead in the series and need two more wins to secure their first franchise title.
body: MILWAUKEE -- The 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are redefining relentless.

They did it again. The Brewers fell behind early and came back to win. This time around, the Rays scored four runs in the first inning and the Brewers just chipped away until they finally (inevitably?) took the lead in the bottom of the seventh inning. They won, 5-4. They are masters of the comeback craft.

It all started in Game 1 of the NLDS. The Padres took the early lead. The Brewers came back to win. It happened again in Game 2. They did it in all four games of the NLCS against the two-time defending champion Dodgers, including a four-run comeback in the Game 4 clincher. And now they've done it again. The Brewers are now 9-1 in the playoffs, and they've come from behind to win seven times.

If that's not enough, some of the other numbers are downright staggering. The Brewers this year, regular season and playoffs combined, are now 41-37 when the other team scores first. That's a mind-boggling stat. The last team to finish a season with a winning record in such situations was the 2009 Yankees (via Sarah Langs).
Or how about this one? The Brewers just became the fifth team in MLB playoff history to win multiple games after falling behind by at least four runs.
These Brewers are also just the third team to trail by four runs at home in the World Series and come back to win, along with the 2017 Astros and 2002 Angels.

"We're down to the end of the season here," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after Game 2 on Saturday. "They're going to tap us on the shoulder here at some point and tell us no more. Guys just, they don't give up. They believe, and they don't give up. They just keep going."

That said, I would be remiss to ignore the other component of World Series Game 2: the mistake-filled game the Rays just played. That absolutely cannot happen against a team as relentless as these Brewers.
- In the bottom of the first inning, Jonathan Aranda botched an attempt to catch a foul ball. William Contreras then singled and the Brewers scored twice that inning.
- In the bottom of the fourth, Aranda let a weak grounder go through his legs. The Brewers scored again, cutting the deficit to 4-3.

- In the top of the sixth, Liam Hicks was thrown out at home plate by Jackson Chourio after a single to left field. It makes sense to try and score the run with two outs, but Hicks was out by a country mile. It was the fourth out on the bases the Rays have made in the World Series. This was only the middle of Game 2.
- Sal Frelick homered to tie the game. He only hit four in the regular season. Give Frelick credit, of course, but that was another thing that just can't happen.

- Chandler Simpson couldn't hold on to a Christian Yelich pop fly in the sixth inning and the dropped ball put runners at first and third with two outs. The play was ruled a single and Tyler Wells got out of the inning, but it should have been caught.
- Not that it mattered much at the time, but the Brewers pulled off a double steal in the eighth, thanks in part to backup catcher Nick Fuentes bobbling the pitch.

"Look, we didn't play our cleanest baseball game by any stretch," Rays manager Kevin Cash said after Game 2. "We pride ourselves on doing everything we can to support the pitchers and making plays behind them. Today was probably not our best day."

The Milwaukee Brewers won 103 games in the regular season and posted the best run differential in baseball. They regularly come from behind to win. They create their own breaks so often. No team can expect to beat them in the playoffs by giving them gifts the way the Rays did in Game 2 of the World Series. It was unacceptable.
Let's not get things twisted, though. The Brewers deserved to win this game and deserve to be up 2-0 in this series, just as they are. They are the better team and have played like it.

Even if that send of Hicks to home was a bad decision, Chourio's throw was excellent, as was the work at home plate by Contreras. Also, the Rays scored four runs in the first inning and didn't score again. That's some outstanding mound work from the Brewers, especially their bullpen. JoJo Romero, Dustin May and DL Hall kept their team in the game before the Brewers tied it and then took the lead and dropped the proverbial hammer with late-inning beasts Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby.

The top of the first inning was a disaster, really, for the Brewers. Logan Henderson gave up four runs in a game for the first time in his (admittedly short) MLB career. Cooper Pratt started the game with a throwing error that opened the door. Hicks crushed a two-run home run to silence the crowd.
But.
And there's always a but with these Brewers, isn't there?

Chourio led off the bottom of the first with a single and the comeback was on. The crowd seemed to sense it was inevitable from the get-go. The noise never wavered. They were electric all night, as if there was never a doubt. For the fans who have watched this team all season, there probably wasn't.

From the press box, the second Sal Frelick hit his unlikely home run, the game seemed over. That blast merely tied the game, but we might as well have called the rest of the thing off. It was over the second that ball crossed over the center field wall. The Rays were cooked because the Brewers are just too good to be allowed to hang around.

Even when the Rays got a leadoff double from Jonny DeLuca in the ninth, it never felt like a huge threat. They even got the runner to third base with Yandy Díaz coming to the plate. No matter. Brewers manager Pat Murphy stuck with Ashby and Ashby got the strikeout.

The Brewers now only need to win two more games before they lose four to secure the first World Series title in franchise history. When they do clinch this thing, it won't be a surprise. It feels inevitable at this point, and if we start to doubt them, they'll remind us with another comeback. That's how relentless they are. No abatement of severity, intensity or strength.

articles.headline: Raleek Brown helps No. 19 Texas Longhorns avoid a devastating loss against No. 7 Ole Miss
keyFacts: No. 19 Texas defeated No. 7 Ole Miss 34-27 to snap a two-legged losing streak and keep playoff hopes alive.
Running back Raleek Brown rushed for 157 yards and the Texas defense intercepted three passes to hold off an Ole Miss rally.
Texas will continue its homestand next week by hosting Mississippi State on Halloween night.
body: Texas Longhorns linebacker Rasheem Biles (3) celebrates an end zone interception with his teammates in the second quarter of the Longhorns' game against the Mississippi Rebels at Royal-Memorial Stadium in Austin, Oct. 24, 2026. (Sara Diggins/Austin American-Statesman)
Needing a win to keep its College Football Playoff hopes alive, the Texas Longhorns managed to secure one Saturday night.

Texas held off an Ole Miss rally and avoided a complete collapse in the second half of a 34-27 win over No. 7 Ole Miss . With the win at Royal-Memorial Stadium, No. 19 Texas (5-2, 2-2) snapped a two-game losing streak.
More: Subscribe to the Statesman's Texas sports newsletter
Saturday's victory was also UT's second over a top-10 opponent this season.

Leading the Longhorns to a victory was running back Raleek Brown, who rushed for 157 yards, and Ryan Wingo, who had 111 receiving yards. The UT defense also intercepted three passes that were thrown by Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, who entered the game as a Heisman Trophy contender, with the last of those turnovers being recorded on the game's final snap.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by hookem.com (@hookemdotcom)
Behind Arch Manning, Texas seizes another double-digit lead

After Ole Miss went 3-and-out on its first drive, the two teams traded field goals. Then things got weird. During a four-play sequence in the first quarter, the following headlines and highlights took place:
Texas offensive lineman Trevor Goosby suffered an apparent leg injury and was carted off the field.
Arch Manning was intercepted by Ole Miss cornerback Jalyn Crawford.
Trinidad Chambliss was intercepted by UT linebacker Justin Cryer.
Texas receiver Cam Coleman dropped what should have been a 59-yard touchdown.

Thanks to a 2-yard touchdown run by Manning – the quarterback's first rushing score of the season – Texas exited the opening frame with a 10-3 lead. The Longhorns then returned to the end zone in the opening minutes of the second quarter during a touchdown drive that featured Manning rushing for 19 yards on a 3rd-and-17 attempt and Ryan Wingo hauling in a 50-yard toss.
More: How Steve Sarkisian, Arch Manning, Texas Longhorns grade in midseason report card

By the end of the first half, Texas had added sophomore running back Michael Terry III's first career touchdown run to the box score and had linebacker Rasheem Biles intercept a 4th-and-goal pass near the goal line in the waning minutes. Those two plays gave UT its largest halftime lead over a ranked opponent since the Longhorns also held a 24-3 edge halfway through their 2024 trip to Michigan.

Texas Longhorns offensive lineman Trevor Goosby (74) leaves the field in a cart after going down with an injury in the first quarter of the Longhorns' game against the Mississippi Rebels at Royal-Memorial Stadium in Austin, Oct. 24, 2026. (Sara Diggins/Austin American-Statesman)
Ole Miss keeps Texas on its heels, but Longhorns survive

Over its past two losses against Oklahoma and Florida, Texas had built 17-7 and 17-3 leads before spoiling both double-digit advantages. So a sold-out crowd at Royal-Memorial Stadium likely didn't feel much relief at halftime despite the Longhorns' 21-point lead.
And it didn't take long for the Rebels to make those fans sweat.

Ole Miss took advantage of Goosby's absence as Blake Purchase blew past Andre Cojoe on the left side of UT's offensive line to sack Manning and force a fumble that the Rebels recovered for a touchdown. Chambliss then threw a 6-yard touchdown pass to make it a 24-17 game with 6:46 left in the third quarter.
More: Photos from DKR as the Longhorns play the Rebels

Ole Miss outscored Texas by 14 points in the third quarter and held the Longhorns to 19 yards of offense. To open the fourth quarter, Chambliss then threw a 27-yard touchdown pass to Horatio Fields to tie the game.

But Texas finally found a spark on offense in the fourth quarter as Texas put together a six-play, 80-yard drive that consisted of all runs and was capped by Manning's 1-yard run on a bootleg. Although Manning got his second touchdown of the day, the biggest plays on that drive were Brown's 47-yard sprint through the Ole Miss defense and a 19-yard gain by Terry.

Texas blocked an Ole Miss field goal on the following drive, and then added Gianni Spetic's 33-yard kick on the other end . The Rebels had one more rally in them, however, and Ole Miss kicked a field goal and then recovered an onside kick in the final minutes. But after Ole Miss drove to UT's 24-yard-line with nine seconds left, Chambliss threw two incomplete passes before Jelani McDonald intercepted an end-zone heave to end the game.

Texas Longhorns quarterback Arch Manning (16) huddles with his team in the second quarter of the Longhorns' game against the Mississippi Rebels at Royal-Memorial Stadium in Austin, Oct. 24, 2026. (Sara Diggins/Austin American-Statesman)
Longhorns to continue homestand next week against Mississippi State

While attempting to build off any momentum that it seized on Saturday night, Texas will return to Royal-Memorial Stadium next weekend for its third straight home game. Mississippi State will be the Longhorns' guest on Halloween night.
More: Texas coach Steve Sarkisian explains why he likes a 24-team CFP
This season, Mississippi State is 4-3 with a 2-3 mark in SEC play. The Bulldogs are coming off a 23-15 loss to Oklahoma this weekend.

Texas owns a 4-2 lead in an all-time series with Mississippi State that dates back to 1921. The Longhorns have beaten Mississippi State in each of the past two seasons, but Texas had to rally to an overtime win in Starkville last year .

articles.headline: O'Shaquie Foster dominates Emanuel Navarrete to become unified junior lightweight champion
keyFacts: O'Shaquie Foster defeated Emanuel Navarrete in San Antonio to become the unified junior lightweight champion.
Foster outlanded Navarrete and scored two knockdowns in the final round to secure a victory by judges' scores.
Foster stated after the fight that he proved he was both the better inside and outside fighter.
body: Performances in battles between champions are rarely more impressive than that which O'Shaquie Foster turned in against Emanuel Navarrete on Saturday in San Antonio. Foster brought the WBC junior lightweight championship to the ring and left with Navarrete's IBF and WBO belts.

Foster set the tone early, leading the dance and picking the right moments to engage while avoiding Navarrete's attempts to push the action with his pressure-based game. In the opening round, Foster was so effective that Navarrete landed no punches in the frame.

While the belief entering the fight was that the fight would ultimately be a battle between Foster's technique and Navarrete's willingness to engage in an ugly fight to land power shots, Foster made it clear as the rounds ticked by that he had no concerns about Navarrete's power, nor was he afraid to stand and put power behind his own shots.

When Navarrete was able to land, Foster was always ready with a response, outlanding Navarrete and doing so with power and grit. It was the kind of performance Foster has always seemed capable of, but rarely displayed, which was why four of his previous five bouts had ended in either a majority or split decision.

Knowing the fight had slipped from his grasp by the championship rounds, Navarrete tried to find a home run shot that could erase the scorecard deficit, and he seemed close to finding that shot when an uppercut rattled Foster late in Round 11.

While it seemed the uppercut may have set up a dramatic charge for Navarrete in the final round, it was Foster who landed a bomb in an exchange, dropping Navarrete to the canvas. While Navarrete attempted to argue that the referee should not have called that moment a knockdown, Foster left no doubt moments later, when another huge right sent Navarrete down for the second time in the round.
Navarrete beat the count and made it to the end of the round, and the fight, but Foster was crowned unified champion by scores of 115-111, 118-108, 118-108.

"I knew he was going to be strong and awkward." Foster said after the fight. "He's a great champion. I just had a little more in me tonight. ... I told y'all before, I felt like I was the better inside fighter and the better outside fighter and I proved that tonight."

articles.headline: Arch Manning, Texas barely save soap opera season with thrilling Ole Miss victory
keyFacts: No. 19 Texas defeated No. 7 Ole Miss 34-27 after holding off a second-half comeback attempt.
Quarterback Arch Manning finished with 212 passing yards, three total touchdowns, two interceptions, and a fumble.
Jelani McDonald secured the game-clinching interception on the final play to preserve the victory for the Longhorns.
body: Arch Manning crossed his arms after a TD run with fireworks exploding in the background. He stomped around the sideline in defiance. He walked into the end zone for the go-ahead TD.
Manning delivered the gotta-have-it game with No. 19 Texas on the brink, even if it was dicey after a second-half comeback by No. 7 Ole Miss. The Longhorns survived in a 34-27 victory.
So, this is what we get after Texas coach Steve Sarkisian described Manning as "edgy" this week? It is worth the experience, right?

Texas (5-2, 2-2 SEC) jumped out to a three-TD lead on the Rebels (5-2, 3-2 SEC). Manning finished 18 of 30 for 212 yards and three total TDs, albeit with two interceptions and a fumble. He summed up that experience in the postgame interview with ESPN's Holly Rowe.
MORE: Which of the SEC 7 two-loss teams has best chance to make CFP?
"I think all week we just said, 'Whatever it takes,' and got the win," Manning said. "I think you need to start doing our games more. We're 3-0 with you this year."

Those three games were decided by a combined total of seven points. The Longhorns held off a furious comeback led by Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, who finished 25 of 52 for 250 yards, two TDs and three interceptions. Chambliss tried to tie the score on the game's final play, but Jelani McDonald, who had the pass breakup on a Hail Mary in the 20-17 victory against Tennessee on Sept. 26, came up with the game-clinching interception.
Manning and Texas remain the soap opera of the 2026 season, and this was yet another cliffhanger for the two-loss Longhorns in the jumbled SEC playoff race.
MORE: Meet Arch Manning's entire extended family
Arch Manning leads Texas to huge halftime lead

Here is what we learned after the Longhorns' victory. Backup quarterback KJ Lacey, who was rumored to be in the mix for more first-team reps in the aftermath of Texas' 27-24 loss to Florida in Week 7, will not be the starter this season. Lacey played one snap after Manning took a hard hit in the third quarter.

Manning transfer rumors, as they have for the past four years, will fizzle again. Manning could still enter the 2027 NFL Draft and be a first-round pick. Texas' season-long script with Manning, in all its drama, is far from finished.

Manning took his own advice and "let it rip" against the Rebels. That started in the first quarter with a 43-yard pass to Ryan Wingo and a 23-yard run by Raleek Brown, who trucked Ole Miss safety Joenel Aguero on the run. Manning scored on a 2-yard run and struck a pose in the end zone.

Manning was not finished. A 19-yard scramble by Manning set up a 50-yard TD pass to Wingo for a 17-3 lead with 12:38 left in the third quarter. Michael Terry III added a 3-yard TD run to extend the lead to 24-3.
ARCH MANNING THROWS HIS FIRST TD OF THE GAME 🔥 (via: @espn) https://t.co/bVuW76eaGV
— The Sporting News (@sportingnews) October 25, 2026

Manning was 13 of 19 for 171 yards, a TD and an interception in the first half. Chambliss was 6 of 18 for 63 yards and two interceptions, including a fourth-and-goal interception to Texas linebacker Rasheem Biles with 1:37 left in the half. This looked like the game where Manning would silence all the critics.
MORE: Where does Steve Sarkisian rank among CFB;s highest paid coaches?
Texas survives wild second half
This is Texas, after all, which was coming off losses to Oklahoma and Florida the last two weeks. The Sooners and Gators outscored the Longhorns 37-14 in the second half over the last two weeks.

Manning lost a fumble on a sack by Blake Purchase, which Kam Franklin recovered in the end zone at the 13:28 mark in the third quarter. The Rebels trimmed the lead to 24-17 on a 6-yard TD pass from Chambliss to Horatio Fields with 6:46 left in the third quarter. The Longhorns had just two first downs in the third quarter.
That set up the fourth quarter. Chambliss tied the score with a 27-yard TD pass to Fields with 13:57 left in the fourth quarter.

Texas answered with a six-play, 80-yard drive that came exclusively on the ground. Brown had a 47-yard run up the middle, which was the Longhorns' first chunk play of the second half. Terry had runs of 19 and 12 yards, respectively, and Manning walked in a 1-yard TD on a bootleg with 8:04 remaining.

— MLFootball (@MLFootball) October 25, 2026
Alex January blocked an Ole Miss field-goal attempt, and Gianni Spetic gave Texas a 34-24 lead on a 33-yard field goal with 2:25 remaining.
You knew it wasn't over. Lucas Carneiro kicked a 39-yard field goal, the Rebels recovered the ensuing onside kick and Chambliss nearly led a game-tying drive before the final interception.
"I was pacing and said a few prayers, but our defense came up clutch," Manning said. "That's what it's all about."
MORE: How a bad day for the Big 12 impacted hurt league's CFP outlook
Is Texas back in the playoff mix?

The Longhorns still have issues. Edge rusher Colin Simmons (ankle) and running back Hollywood Smothers (shoulder) missed Saturday's game. Tackle Trevor Goosby was carted off with an injury in the first quarter, and receiver Cam Coleman left with a shoulder injury in the third quarter. Texas had 14 penalties for 134 yards.

Yet if the College Football Playoff rankings came out Tuesday, the Longhorns would probably be in the top 12 based on victories against Ole Miss, No. 3 Ohio State and No. 11 Tennessee. No other team has three victories against teams inside the top 12 at this point.

We'll find out more over the next two weeks in road games against No. 22 Missouri and No. 18 LSU. Texas needs even more out of Manning; otherwise, the doom-and-gloom cycle will start again with a third loss. Is there a more entertaining drama in college football right now?

articles.headline: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
keyFacts: Nearly 1,000 people were arrested following clashes during mass demonstrations across France on Saturday, officials said.
Hundreds of thousands protested over the cost of living and poor school conditions, prompting the deployment of 70,000 police officers.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the number of arrests would increase following Saturday's clashes.
body: - Published
Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.

After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.

Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.

President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.

Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.

French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.

In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.

"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
NuÃ±ez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.
The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.

Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of OrlÃ©ans which proceeded peacefully.
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Barcelona, more than 100 people were arrested after a student protest descended into what local authorities described as "gratuitous violence".
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.

In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.

Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.

Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

articles.headline: Brewers erase four-run deficit to stun Rays and take 2-0 World Series lead
keyFacts: The Milwaukee Brewers overcame a four-run deficit to defeat the Tampa Bay Rays 5-4 on Saturday, taking a 2-0 lead in the World Series.
Sal Frelick tied the score with a home run in the sixth inning, and Cooper Pratt hit the go-ahead single in the seventh.
Game 3 of the series is scheduled for Monday night at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg, Florida.
body: Sal Frelick tied the score with his first home run in three months, Cooper Pratt hit a go-ahead single in the seventh inning and the Milwaukee Brewers stunned the Tampa Bay Rays 5-4 on Saturday night for a 2-0 World Series lead by overcoming a four-run deficit for the second time in the postseason.
Tampa Bay, who won the AL pennant by forcing opponents into mistakes, committed one error, made two other misplays that could have been charged as errors and had a runner thrown out at the plate.

Down 4-0 in the first inning, Milwaukee rallied for their seventh comeback win of this postseason. The Brewers also rebounded from a 4-0 deficit to beat the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 in Game 4 of the NL Championship Series, completing a four-game sweep.
After losing Friday’s opener 3-2, the Rays burst ahead against rookie Logan Henderson but the Brewers started to claw back with two runs in the bottom half against Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen.

David Hamilton cut the deficit to 4-3 with a run-scoring grounder in the fourth and Frelick capped a nine-pitch at-bat against Ian Seymour in the sixth by driving a fastball over the center-field fence.

Frelick had gone 103 plate appearances without a home run since his 11 July drive off Pittsburgh’s Braxton Ashcraft and had not gone deep against a left-handed pitcher since opening day against Tyler Gilbert of the Chicago White Sox. Frelick sped around the bases in 18.72 seconds, half the time of some theatrical trots this postseason.

Screaming fans at the second game of Milwaukee’s first World Series since 1982 were fired up during the seventh-inning stretch, dancing to the Beer Barrel Polka played by Mike Schneider, an accordionist from Clinton, Wisconsin.

Brice Turang doubled against losing pitcher Tyler Wells on the second pitch of the bottom half, advanced on Garrett Mitchell’s flyout to right and scored when Pratt, a 22-year-old who debuted in June, looped a sinker from Kevin Kelly into short right field.
Abner Uribe pitched one and one-third hitless innings for the win.

Jonny DeLuca doubled off Aaron Ashby starting the ninth, then Victor Mesa Jr struck out when he couldn’t check his swing. Pinch-hitter Ben Williamson’s groundout advanced the runner and Yandy Díaz struck out when he couldn’t check his swing on a full-count pitch.
Ashby has three saves in the postseason while not allowing a run.
Milwaukee won their seventh straight game, becoming the fifth team to twice overcome four-run deficits for victories in a single postseason and the first since Philadelphia in 2022.
Game 3 of the matchup between teams seeking their first title is Monday night at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg, Florida, where the Brewers last played in 2023.
Of the 57 previous teams to take 2-0 World Series leads, 46 claimed the championship.
Tampa Bay took a 4-2 lead in the highest-scoring Series first inning since Game 4 in 1993 as the teams combined for seven hits, tying the most in an opening frame.

Still, Milwaukee improved to 13-0 in games started by Henderson, dating to his 2025 debut. He followed Jacob Misiorowski in the Brewers’ rotation, the first time teammates aged 24 or younger started the first two games of the Series since Cincinnati’s Gary Nolan and Ross Grimsley in 1972.
Henderson started on 11 days’ rest and struggled as the Rays fouled off 13 of 35 pitches in the first. He gave up four runs – three earned – in three innings.
Given an extra day of rest, Rasmussen allowed three runs and six hits over three and two-thirds innings in his shortest start since 9 July.

Pratt made his fourth error of the postseason at shortstop, the Brewers’ ninth in 10 games, bouncing his throw past first baseman Jake Bauers on a leadoff grounder by Díaz. Chandler Simpson and Junior Caminero followed with RBI singles, and Liam Hicks hit a two-run homer.
Jackson Chourio and Bauers started the bottom half with singles and first baseman Jonathan Aranda allowed Contreras’ one-out foul pop to bounce out of his mitt near netting in front of the seats.

With Bauers running on a full-count pitch, Contreras bounced an RBI single to the left of second baseman Richie Palacios, who had taken a step toward the base. Mitchell’s two-out single cut the deficit to 4-2.
Hamilton hit an RBI grounder in the fourth that bounced under Aranda’s legs for an error.
Chourio threw out Hicks from left for the final out of the sixth when third base coach Brady Williams waved the slow-footed catcher to try to score from second on Mesa’s single.

articles.headline: Obama joins El-Sayed in Michigan rally cry before key midterms
keyFacts: Former US President Barack Obama joined Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a Detroit rally ahead of key midterms.
Black residents make up about 75 percent of Detroit's population.
Obama denounced attempts to portray candidates as un-American over their faith or background.
body: Obama joins El-Sayed in Michigan rally cry before key midterms

Former US President Barack Obama joined Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a Detroit rally ahead of key midterms. With Black residents making up about 75% of Detroit’s population, Obama denounced attempts to portray candidates as un-American over their faith or background.

articles.headline: Forget Tom Cruise, Sci-Fi's Foundational 1950s Classic Movie Is Free to Watch on YouTube
keyFacts: The 1953 film adaptation of The War of the Worlds is currently available to watch for free on YouTube.
Polygon reported that a 2025 adaptation of the story has been widely criticized and compared to an Amazon advertisement.
The 1953 movie relocates H.G. Wells' story to California and follows a physicist and a local resident during a Martian invasion.
body: H.G. Wells' The War of the Worlds is a punchline now, and it's Amazon's fault. At time of writing, the newest adaptation of The War of the Worlds is a "screenlife" movie from 2025 that’s a frontrunner for the worst film of the 21st century.

War of the Worlds 2025 is worth watching once, if only to marvel at how its creators consistently made the dumbest possible choices at every opportunity, up to and including its metamorphosis into an ad for Amazon drone delivery in its final act. Even so, it isn't bad in the right way to be funny. It's bad in the way that makes you want to comb through it looking for the black box. You want to know why this happened, so the appropriate authorities can stop it from happening again.

That probably means it's going to be a while before we see another adaptation of The War of the Worlds. It'll take time for the Amazon stink to wear off. For now, that means the long history of War of the Worlds has a strange capstone on it.

Wells' 1898 novel isn't the first alien invasion story in the Western canon, but it's often credited with cementing the concept in the popular imagination. Naturally, that's led to multiple adaptations in the 128 years since it was published, with creators from Orson Welles to Steven Spielberg to the Asylum all taking their own swings at the material. The most famous version of The War of the Worlds is still likely Welles' 1938 radio play, which triggered a panic on its first broadcast by accidentally convincing some listeners that it was a live news program.

The first film adaptation of The War in the Worlds came out in 1953, starring Gene Barry and Ann Robinson, directed by Byron Haskin, and written by Barré Lyndon. It moves the setting from 1890s England to 1950s California and accelerates its pace, which turns Wells' story of the near-fall of humanity into an 85-minute war movie. 1953’s The War of the Worlds is currently free (and colorized) on YouTube, if you're interested in putting an old-school alien invasion on your Halloween viewing schedule.
Intellects vast and cool and unsympathetic

Haskin's War of the Worlds begins when a rain of strange meteors land all over the world. One hits near a small town in California, where physicist Dr. Clayton Forrester (Barry; and yes, the MST3K mad scientist was named after the War of the Worlds character) is on hand to investigate. He deduces the meteor must be hollow, but it's still too hot from reentry for him to get any closer.

Later that night, the meteor reveals itself as an alien "cylinder" from Mars, which studies the world through electronic eyes on flexible metal stalks. When three locals try to make peaceful contact, the cylinder immediately incinerates them with a heat ray, then proceeds to lay waste to any other humans it sees. There was no miscommunication, and this wasn’t any human’s fault. The Martians came to clean human life off the face of Earth.

After an initial disastrous exchange between the U.S. Army and the cylinders, Forrester flees the scene alongside local resident Sylvia (Robinson). As the U.S. military tries to defend against the Martians, who initially seem invincible, we follow Forrester and Sylvia through the battles and their aftermath.

Like many other science fiction movies from the 1950s, you do have to meet The War of the Worlds halfway. Its special effects were groundbreaking at the time of its release, which earned the film an Oscar, but they border on quaint now, especially in modern restorations. The movie was simply never meant to be watched in higher resolutions.

If you can suspend your disbelief, it's easy to see why audiences in the '50s thought The War of the Worlds was horrifying. The Martians' heat rays make people flash and disappear, replaced by man-shaped piles of ash. It’s a simple effect, but it’s still creepy, if only because the cylinders wield the heat rays like they're weeding a garden.

The first major conflict between the Martians and the U.S. military in The War of the Worlds is a nightmare of men and machines being blasted into nothing. The military’s leaders move fast, listen to reason, do everything right, and still have no chance at all. The movie is punctuated by reports from outside the U.S. of other nations losing cities and battles, unceremoniously swept off the map by the cylinders. This isn't a war; it's a disaster movie, and the disaster is winning.

There's a bleak power to The War of the Worlds that must've hit even harder during the Cold War. Watching it now, it’s still got some of that impact, in ways that almost remind me of cosmic horror. It's easy now to mock it for its early effects work, but if you can meet The War of the Worlds where it lives, you’ll see why it's become a sci-fi/horror classic.
The War of the Worlds (1953) is now streaming on YouTube.

articles.headline: Iran says U.S. military not allowed in Gulf "under any circumstance"
keyFacts: Iran warned Saturday that U.S. ships would never be allowed in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances as regional tensions continued mounting.
The Saudi-led coalition announced it intercepted a ballistic missile launched by Houthi militants toward Riyadh, while the Houthis launched multiple regional attacks.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian stated that many Iranians are struggling to afford food due to the ongoing economic pressures from the war.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Iran warned on Saturday that U.S. ships would never be allowed in the Persian Gulf "under any circumstances," as tensions between Tehran and Washington continue mounting. Both sides have signalled a possible return to strikes, with the U.S. ambassador to Turkey warning Iran could be struck as soon as this weekend.

- Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
- U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has told the Financial Times the could last another year, but Waltz said he hopes the Iranians "come to the table" before that.
Saudis intercept ballistic missile launched by Houthis toward Riyadh, officials say
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthi militants said early Sunday local time it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group toward the Saudi capital of Riyadh.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Prior to the coalition's statement, an Agence France-Presse journalist reported that three explosions had rung out in Riyadh.
The blasts came after residents received alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
Ayatollah meets with head of Iranian judiciary, focuses on compensation for war damage

Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has still not been seen in public since the beginning of the war, met with Hujjat al-Islam Mohseni Ejei, the head of Iran's judiciary, to discuss a range of issues on Saturday.

Most interestingly, in connection to the war, a readout of the meeting on X said Iran was committed to "resolutely pursuing compensation for material and moral damages arising from the crimes committed by" the U.S. and Israel.
One of Iran's demands in the past as part of a peace agreement was the U.S. would have to pay to rebuild much of the damage in the country. The demand was dismissed by the U.S.
While not specific, the statement also said they discussed "making the fullest possible use of modern technologies."

Khamenei was injured in a strike on the palace that killed his father, the Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The strike on the first day of the war also killed the leader's daughter, granddaughter, son-in-law and daughter-in-law. Mojtaba Khamenei survived though he's been in hiding ever since the strike.
Iran remains open to talks with U.S. under Pakistan-brokered deal, envoy says

Iran remains open to talks with the U.S. under a Pakistan-brokered interim deal reached in June to end the conflict, Tehran's ambassador to Islamabad said Saturday, accusing Washington of undermining diplomacy and prolonging the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.

Ambassador Reza Amiri Moghadam said Iran recently conveyed through Pakistan it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, but accused President Trump of rejecting the proposal by insisting the blockade of Iranian ports would continue.

Pakistan and Qatar helped broker the June agreement, which sought to restore shipping through the strait, lift the U.S. naval blockade and begin negotiations toward a broader deal addressing Iran's nuclear program.

Moghadam, speaking at a seminar in Islamabad, said Iranian officials had conveyed their willingness to reopen the strait during visits to Tehran by Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, provided Washington ended its blockade.

Moghadam also said Tehran would study the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement that includes Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey before deciding whether to support it, describing it as a potential instrument for unity. "We will study the Mecca Agreement, and if it is good, we will support it," he said.
Iran president admits many struggling for food as war, sanctions take toll
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Saturday many Iranians were struggling to put food on the table, as economic pressure from the war with the United States mounts.

The U.S. has in recent weeks dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure, while Iran's leaders have said peace negotiations will only succeed without pressure and threats from Washington as the conflict remains locked in a stalemate.

"There are many people in this society who are struggling to put food on the table because of the war we have found ourselves in, because of the wartime conditions we are living under," Pezeshkian said in a speech shared on his website.
Pezeshkian called for an end to what he described as a "state of neither war nor peace", saying Tehran "must also get out of this situation," without specifying how.
His remarks came as fears of renewed fighting grew. On Friday, U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack said U.S. strikes on Iran could resume as soon as this weekend.
"Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely," Barrack told podcast host Mario Nawfal. Barrack, who also serves as Washington's envoy on Syria, does not have a direct role on Iran.
AFP/CBS
Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia, Yemen's Aden after deadly strikes

Yemen's Houthi militant group launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen's internationally-recognized government on Saturday after blaming the kingdom for strikes that the Iran-backed group said killed 17 people.
Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attacks in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer.
Over the past 24 hours, the Yemeni fighters said they targeted three Saudi airports including the international airport in capital Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.

Military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched missiles at "King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of the Saudi enemy, in two phases", the airports in Dammam in the east and Najran in the south.

The international airport on Saturday however said it would resume domestic and international flights "effective Sunday" in a post on X, after it was closed following several deadly attacks this month.
The Houthis also launched attacks on the southern Khamis Mushait air base as well as "crude oil pumping stations and the crude oil pipeline from east to west."

The Saudi civil defense agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles. The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie."
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.

The fresh attack claims came after the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel accused the kingdom of separate strikes in Yemen that killed more than a dozen people. Riyadh has not claimed the alleged strikes.

Yemen's civil war, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis against the Saudi-supported and internationally recognized-government, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war has roiled the region.
State Department updates travel advisories for 14 countries in Middle East
The U.S. State Department has updated travel advisories for 14 countries in the Middle East "to reflect the threat of Iranian-supported Houthi regional aggression."

The advisories also follow from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warning of Iranian plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and elsewhere.
The warnings come as the Trump administration weighs whether to restart military strikes against Iran, and whether to provide air support to Saudi forces confronting the Houthis.
U.S. threats toward Iran "largely for media consumption," IRGC official says

An official with Iran's Revolutionary Guard took a swipe at the U.S. and President Trump's repeated threats, calling them "largely for media consumption" and saying the country is ready if there are renewed hostilities.

"The enemy itself knows better than anyone that it cannot carry out effective operations under current conditions and will certainly fail to achieve its objectives," IRGC spokesperson Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi told semi-official Fars news agency on Saturday.

Mr. Trump has said any possible strikes on Iran will wait until after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, but he has repeatedly said he could end the war with Iran any time he wants through renewed military action.
Mohebbi said Iran will be ready if the U.S. does return to military strikes.
"Even if the enemy undertakes limited action, Iran's response will be several times greater, given the existing state of readiness and the operational plans of the armed forces," he said.
UAE closes beaches after oil spill from tanker
The United Arab Emirates has closed beaches and warned fishermen to avoid parts of its Gulf shores after an oil spill from a tanker.

The spill impacted the beaches of Umm Al Quwain, one of the seven emirates making up the federation, and cleanup efforts were underway, the Climate Change and Environment Ministry said. Images obtained by AP showed oil washing up along the beach in Umm Al Quwain.
The ministry said the spill poses no health risks but did not provide details about the scale of the leak.

The spill came two weeks after Iran's state-run broadcaster reported an oil tanker had struck a naval mine and caught fire while attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz without coordinating with Iran.
Airstrikes kill 9 people in Yemen, including women and children, Houthis say
Two days of strikes on Yemen have killed nine people including women and children, according to the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
Two separate strikes killed five people, including a woman and child, in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Saturday, according to the Houthi-run Health Ministry.

Also Saturday, the Houthi media center said a wave of strikes struck the coastal city of Mokha in Taiz province, which the Houthis captured in early September. The center didn't provide details on what was struck and The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the Houthi claims.

On Friday, an airstrike killed four people — two women and two children — from the same family when it struck a house in the town of Hiba near the city of Taiz, a hotbed of violence in the country's revived civil war.
The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the strikes, which came as fighting between the kingdom and the Iranian-backed rebels has escalated. Saudi Arabia did not respond to a request for comment.
Saudi forces intercept Houthi missiles targeting oil hub Yanbu, Taif
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen announced on Saturday it had intercepted two missiles fired by the Houthis toward Taif and Yanbu, in the kingdom's west.
It came shortly after Riyadh's civil defence agency broadcast warnings of "potential danger" for four western regions, including Taif and Yanbu as well Mecca, home to Islam's holiest city, and Yanbu.
The alerts were all rescinded minutes later.

Residents were instructed to "proceed to the nearest safe place" by the agency. The agency also repeated a legal warning against sharing images or information related to "countering missiles and drones."
The Gulf kingdom has come under repeated attack from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis in recent weeks as part of the latter country's revived civil war.
Yanbu is a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast that has allowed Riyadh to bypass Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz for much of its crude exports.
Iran warns U.S. ships would never be allowed in the Gulf
Iran said on Saturday that U.S. ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and President Trump will "take that dream to his grave".

The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as U.S. ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weekend.
"We will not allow U.S. military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
"The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave."
CBS/AFP
Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.

The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.

The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.

Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
U.S. to reduce staffing at 4 embassies in Middle East
The U.S. State Department says it will reduce staffing at four U.S. embassies in the Middle East, not including Saudi Arabia, where nonessential diplomats and family members earlier this week.

The staffing changes — driven by concerns that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants may escalate rocket, missile and drone attacks around the region — will affect the embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, but do not entail an order to leave, the department said.
The embassies involved are all under what is known as "restricted operations" status that has already reduced the size of their personnel footprints. The embassies will remain open.

On Wednesday, a U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News that the U.S. military had been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
CBS/AP
Iranian president to meet with Putin next week in Moscow
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will travel to Moscow next week for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, according to a report by Reuters.
It hasn't been long since Pezeshkian spoke to Putin in person, but this will be the first meeting between the two in Russia during the ongoing war.
The two leaders met with each other on the sidelines of the Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan on Oct. 8. The two also met at a summit in Kyrgyzstan in September.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Tehran earlier this week as the two sides continue to strengthen relations. Araghchi said Russia and Iran were closer than ever, despite President Trump saying Russia was doing little to help Iran a day prior.
U.N. sounds alarm on besieged Yemen city of Taiz
Time is running out to get aid into Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching Yemen's third-largest city, the United Nations said Friday.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government.
"Safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access is urgently needed so that essential supplies and life-saving assistance can reach people in need," said the U.N. humanitarian agency OCHA.
"It's 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off," said OCHA spokesman Jens Laerke.
"We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out," he told a press conference in Geneva.
Laerke said the dwindling water supply was a growing concern, as most residents depended on water brought in by trucks.
"With the roads closed and the diesel to run the trucks very scarce, water production in the city has fallen by about half," he said.
U.S. envoy leaves open possibility of striking Iran this weekend, despite Trump's prior midterm promise

A U.S. official left open the door for the possibility of a strike on Iran this weekend, despite President Trump previously saying there would be none before the midterm elections in less than two weeks.

"Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely," Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and point man on Syria, who does not have a direct role on Iran policy, told Israeli army radio in response to a question.
"(President Trump) is very clear. He's open and available and accessible to a deal and we've been at the table for months and months and months," Barrack said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections Tuesday, in recent days has repeatedly vowed to topple the clerical state in Iran, following two major bombing campaigns against Iran since last year.
Mr. Trump has also signaled an openness to resuming strikes on Iran after a long deadlock in diplomacy although he earlier said it would not happen before midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Earlier Friday, Mr. Trump repeated a common refrain that the U.S. could choose to end the war anytime it wants through a renewed military campaign, but could also let the country "wither" under sanctions.
AFP/CBS
European, Mideast foreign ministers push peace and diplomacy at Istanbul talks

Foreign ministers from eight European and Middle Eastern countries met in Istanbul on Friday in an unprecedented format, urging diplomacy and peaceful solutions to prevail across the Middle East as well as the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Ministers from Britain, France, Germany and Italy met counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss Hormuz — a crucial trade route blocked in the Iran war — as well as Yemen and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

At the heart of the talks was the situation in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, which is paralyzing global trade and driving up energy prices as well as the attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthis from Yemen, allies of Tehran.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said a new escalation between Iran and the United States "would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices."
"The first thing this group of eight countries ... will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region," he told journalists.
Italy's Antonio Tajani said the regional problem cannot be solved "from a purely military standpoint."
Wall Street mostly loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
Stocks slipped Friday on Wall Street under increasing pressure from rising oil prices.

The S&P 500 fell 0.2%, adding to its decline from a day before. The index is on track for a second-straight week of losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 550 points, or just over 1%, as of 11:50 a.m. Eastern time.
The Nasdaq composite rose 0.2%, bolstered by gains for several big tech stocks that also helped ease losses elsewhere.

Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the broader market, where three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.5% to over $117. It has surged from less than $97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since March.
Trump says U.S. could take all of Iran's oil: "We could take the whole country"
President Trump delivered a familiar message on Iran as he left the White House for a trip to rally voters in Florida, but also added the U.S. could take all of Iran's oil if we wanted to.
"Iran is not able to do much now. And we could, if we wanted to, just take all of the oil," Mr. Trump said. "We could take the whole country."
"And as you know, the Hormuz Strait is ours, and that's the way we'll keep it," the president added.

Mr. Trump was also asked about U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz saying the war with Iran could drag on for another year, while the president has said for months the war will end "very soon."
"We could end it very quickly," Mr. Trump said. "But Iran is a failing nation. We're taking all the oil out that we want."
"The question is, 'Do we want to finish it off or do we just want to let it wither?' Because we're getting everything we wanted," he said.
Tanker involved in UAE oil spill identified, analysts say
The tanker involved in an oil spill off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has been identified, according to analysts who spoke to the Reuters new agency.
Emirati authorities have not named the vessel, but Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, told Reuters the oil slick was coming from a vessel called the Gem No. 2.
Another analyst told the news agency that satellite imagery appears to show a large spill coming from the tanker.

"The slick is considerably larger, covering approximately 160 square km (60 square miles), and looks to be coming from the ship," Leon Moreland, a researcher at the Conflict and Environment Observatory, said.
"Furthermore, a slick this close to shore increases the chance it could impact nearby beaches and ecologically sensitive habitats," he said.
The Gem No. 2 was hit by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE on Oct. 9, shipping sources told Reuters.
No group claimed responsibility for the incident at the time, but maritime security sources told the news agency that it took place outside of the Strait of Hormuz.
Further escalation between Iran and the U.S. "would leave no winners," French foreign minister says
Any further escalation between Iran and the U.S. "would leave no winners," France's foreign minister said Friday.

Speaking to reporters in Istanbul after a meeting with foreign ministers from the U.K., Germany, Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Jean-Noel Barrot said that "a further escalation between Iran and the United States would leave no winners and would likely have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices," according to remarks reported by the Reuters news agency.
UAE resident describes smelling gas after oil tanker spill
Residents in the north of the United Arab Emirates have described smelling gas after an oil spill off the country's coastline.
Many Emiratis have reported chemical smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai, the largest city in the UAE.
"For the past two days it smelled like 10 gas stations spilled their gas everywhere," a Sharjah resident told the AFP news agency, asking to remain anonymous.
"I was on my balcony and panicked thinking gas was leaking in my house and I will blow up everyone."
Emirati authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement Friday, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.

News of the spill came a day after Iran claimed to have struck four commercial vessels in Persian Gulf waters and said three others had hit sea mines in the region, though President Trump has accused Tehran of making up the incidents to drive up oil prices.
CBS/AFP
Iranian state TV claims movement of "non-compliant" vessels in Strait of Hormuz completely halted

Iranian state TV claimed Friday, citing an unnamed source close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy, that all movement of "non-compliant" vessels through the Strait of Hormuz had been completely halted following a series of Iranian attacks on ships and navigational support systems.

The report cited the source as saying that if U.S. military escorts and ship-to-ship transfers - all of which the Iranian regime refers to as "oil smuggling" - resumes, action against the vessels and technical systems supporting them will be "much more forceful."

Iran has repeatedly warned commercial ships not to use the long-established shipping lanes through the strait, through which about 20% of global oil supplies passed before the war. Tehran demands that all vessels seek authorization and use a northern route, close to its coast, and it has attacked ships for months that refuse.
The Trump administration, however, has encouraged shippers to use an alternative southern route, close to Oman, to avoid Iranian tolls.
Iran claimed Thursday to have struck four ships that used that route, and said three others hit sea mines in the U.S.-designated shipping lanes.
President Trump on Thursday dismissed Iranian claims about striking vessels as lies aimed at increasing global oil prices ahead of the looming U.S. midterm elections.
Both Iran and the U.S. have claimed at various times during the war to have completely halted traffic that violates their respective blockades of the waterway.
Iran's foreign minister calls Israel's relationship with the U.S. "parasitic"
Iran's foreign minister has called Israel's relationship with the United States "parasitic," citing alleged American taxpayer funding for missile defense in Israel.

"The U.S. has over the past three years spent $11 BILLION in taxpayer money on missile defense for Israel," Abbas Araghchi wrote Friday in a post on X, citing calculations by independent policy analyst Stephen Semler, who said he arrived at the number using Pentagon budget documents, media reports, and open-source intelligence.
CBS News has not been able to independently verify the figures.

Semler is the founder of the Security Policy Reform Institute, a think tank that, according to its website, is "driven by empiricism and guided by progressive values" to promote "the meaningful reform of U.S. foreign policy to break the cycle of endless war and serve the most pressing economic, social, and political needs of working-class Americans."

Araghchi also said the U.S. had "fired more interceptors defending Israel than Israel has," a claim supported by a Washington Post story from May that cited U.S. Defense Department data and U.S. officials.
"That is not a symbiotic relationship," Araghchi said. "It is a parasitic one."
UAE reports oil spill from tanker

The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast Friday, a day after Iran claimed to have struck four commercial vessels in Persian Gulf waters and said three others had hit sea mines in the region.
Emirati authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation ... to limit environmental impacts," adding that Umm Al Quwain beaches had been closed.
Many residents in the north of the UAE have reported oil smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai.
Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States.

The British maritime security UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel was hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control. According to the maritime security company Vanguard, the vessel in question was the Panama-flagged oil tanker GEM NO.2.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed the seven additional incidents on Thursday, but none have been corroborated thus far, and President Trump accused Tehran of inventing strikes on ships to drive up oil prices.
CBS/AFP
Saudi Arabia postpones U.N. summit in Riyadh amid Houthi strikes
Saudi Arabia has postponed the sixth U.N. World Data Forum and the second Saudi Statistical Forum, which had been scheduled to take place in Riyadh next month, until 2027.
The kingdom's General Authority for Statistics said the delay was intended to ensure broad international participation.
It comes after the recent rescheduling of Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative, known as "Davos in the Desert," which was also pushed back to 2027 amid escalating regional tension and .
U.S. ambassador to the U.N. says Iran war could last another year
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has said the war with Iran could drag on for another year.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Friday, Waltz said the U.S. could still be fighting the war President Trump initially said would last "" 12 months from now.
Waltz told the FT the U.S. will not have achieved its key goals in Iran until the country disposes of its highly enriched uranium and accepts a "meaningful agreement on their domestic enrichment."
"I'm not going to put out hypotheticals. One would hope that they'll come to the table in a meaningful way before that," Waltz said, referring to the possibility of another year of war.

He added that Mr. Trump "and the U.S. Navy can maintain this blockade [on Iranian ports] for the foreseeable future," and said the administration was still "tightening" its economic pressure campaign against Iran.
Mr. Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have renewed their threats to launch new strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Foreign ministers from Europe and Gulf region to discuss Strait of Hormuz and Iran conflict

Foreign ministers from seven nations in Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere will hold talks in Istanbul Friday focused on the Strait of Hormuz and the interlinked crises in the Middle East, as well as the Ukraine war.

Ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group, composed of Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, to discuss the Israel-Palestinian crisis, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source told AFP.

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband's office said the talks would revolve around "the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia," as the in its decade-long civil war, which has flared up amid the U.S. war on Iran.

"Despite positive progress from the U.S. and regional partners, passage through the Strait remains under threat, with traffic through the waterway sharply down on pre-war levels," a U.K. foreign ministry statement said.

It said Miliband would "advocate for a diplomatic solution to the crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms" and stress "how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal."
"The U.K. is stepping up to help stabilize the region, having this week committed RAF Typhoons to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks in their airspace," it added.
CBS/AFP
Saudi Aramco says volume bypassing Strait of Hormuz via pipeline has surged

The president of Saudi state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco, whose facilities have been targeted by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants repeatedly for weeks, says the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has more than tripled.
The East-West pipeline's capacity has surged from 2 million to 7 million barrels each day, President and CEO Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business.

Built in the early 1980s, the pipeline has played a crucial role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil amid disruption to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. It carries crude from Saudi oil fields and production facilities in the east, on the Persian Gulf, to the Yanbu oil terminal on the Saudi Red Sea coast on the other side of the vast kingdom, from which it can be shipped to global markets.

That route, which, unlike the Gulf, has two available exits, has also been threatened and attacked by the Houthis, who have vowed to stop Saudi shipments via the Red Sea's southern gateway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Nasser said Saudi Aramco has used drones to assess damage caused to infrastructure, including sites key to the East-West pipeline, by Houthi attacks, and to help with firefighting.
CBS/AP
Trump accuses Iran of lying about strikes on ships to drive up oil prices
As crude oil prices hit their highest levels since May, President Trump accused Iran on Thursday of lying about attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up global energy prices.

"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Brent crude, the international standard for oil, hit $112 a barrel Thursday morning, its highest price since May 18.

Iran claimed to have struck four vessels in the Persian Gulf Thursday after they transited the Strait of Hormuz using a U.S.-endorsed route that Tehran rejects, and it said three others hit sea mines in the region after using the same shipping lanes. All of the ships were damaged along or after using southern shipping lanes in the strait near the Omani coast, which the Trump administration has insisted for weeks is open to traffic.

The U.S. military has escorted tankers out of the Persian Gulf using that route, boosting the quantity of oil leaving the region, but it is a costly process. Overall instability in the Middle East has kept energy prices high despite the recently increased supplies.

articles.headline: Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday to elect their next president
keyFacts: Brazilians will vote on Sunday in a presidential runoff election between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro holds a one percentage point lead over Lula in recent polls, according to Reuters.
Roughly 160 million people are expected to vote on Sunday to elect the nation's next president.
body: Brazilians will vote for their next president on Sunday after neither 80-year-old incumbent left-winger Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva nor right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro garnered a majority of the votes in the election’s first round earlier this month.

Bolsonaro, who has President Donald Trump’s endorsement, is the slight favorite heading into Sunday’s runoff, with him leading by roughly one percentage point in the most recent polls released on Saturday, according to Reuters . The two candidates finalized the arguments of their campaigns on Saturday, as Lula marched along Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana beach, while Bolsonaro campaigned in a key battleground state.

Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, was the president of Brazil from 2019 to 2023 and is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of plotting a coup after his 2022 loss. His son largely took over his political empire. A current senator, Bolsonaro beat Lula by five percentage points in the first round of voting.
BRAZIL HEADS TO A RUNOFF ELECTION AFTER BOLSONARO AND LULA FAIL TO GARNER A MAJORITY OF VOTES

Bolsonaro winning would likely lead to a closer relationship between the United States and Brazil. Trump has built strong relationships with other right-wing Latin American leaders, such as Argentinian President Javier Milei and Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele.

“The time is almost here,” Bolsonaro said in a social media video on Sunday. “There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years.” Bolsonaro’s campaign centers on tax cuts and cracking down on crime, and roughly 160 million people are expected to vote on Sunday.

articles.headline: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida

body: WEST PALM BEACH (AP) — President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday, saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.

Trump and first lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office together after the president spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Trump has been criticized in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots.
Asked if he voted the party line, Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said, “Very much so.”

Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy . The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.

Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
As for the war in Iran, he said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”

Melania Trump , who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine.
“We will see,” she told reporters.
TRUMP AND THE MAGA ENTHUSIASM STRATEGY
In Florida, Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly , a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat , to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.
